articles.title_orig: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on Friday accused President Donald Trump of putting US national security at risk by allowing advanced artificial intelligence chips to be exported to Chinese companies, including those with alleged ties to China's military.
Speaking on the Senate floor, Schumer cited information released by the House of Representatives showing that the Trump administration approved nearly 900,000 shipments of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies during the first six months after easing export restrictions.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday disclosed that the Commerce Department approved 879,000 shipments of advanced Nvidia and AMD chips between December 2025 and May 2026.
The shipments included 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all of which the Pentagon lists as companies allegedly linked to the Chinese military, according to the House committee.
Schumer alleged that the Commerce Department authorized the sale of tens of thousands of Nvidia chips to a company affiliated with a Chinese intelligence operative who had previously targeted former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Last week, Huang resigned after 33 years as CEO, following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick knew about the woman's alleged intelligence ties before the sales were approved, according to Schumer.
"Keep in mind, Trump and Lutnick knew this woman was a spy ahead of time, and still rushed to approve the sale of this sensitive technology to her companies," he said.
"Trump and Lutnick sold out America's national security to make a quick buck for themselves and their billionaire buddies," said Schumer, accusing the administration of prioritizing financial interests over US security and technological competitiveness.
The Democratic leader also criticized Trump's reception this week by Chinese officials, arguing that Beijing's warm welcome was connected to the administration's decision to loosen restrictions on advanced American semiconductor exports.
"Trump needs to realize that the only reason he received such a warm welcome from the Chinese Communist Party this week was because he's doling out our most advanced AI chips to China, like their party favors," he said.
Schumer urged Congress to pass three pieces of legislation to tighten oversight of AI chip exports: the AI Overwatch Act, the MATCH Act, and the Chips Security Act.
Schumer is seeking the post of Senate majority leader in the new Congress starting in January, in which Democrats are set to enjoy a 56-44 Senate majority over Republicans. One senator, Chris Van Hollen, is challenging Schumer for the job.
Democrats have pledged to carry out more vigorous oversight of the Trump administration once they take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate on Jan. 3.

articles.title_orig: Fresh off China trip, Trump bobs and weaves in freewheeling press conference
articles.title_zh: Fresh off China trip, Trump bobs and weaves in freewheeling press conference
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles land in Poland, as Europe held military drills nearby. NATO calls it a violation
articles.content_orig:
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near MoÅodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa DÄba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
The UK defence secretary toured the site of the Koalicja operation with four other European colleagues
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Dutch court bars Chinese SUV in Europe over resemblance to Land Rover Defender
articles.title_zh: Dutch court bars Chinese SUV in Europe over resemblance to Land Rover Defender
articles.content_orig:
By FREDA LEWIS-STEMPEL, SENIOR MOTORING REPORTER
Updated: 05:34 EST, 20 November 2026
One of China's newest luxury car brands has proven its off-roading might by getting its range-topping SUV to tow a jumbo jet.
Denza – the luxury technology sub-brand of BYD – used its Bao 5 boxy SUV to pull the famous airliner – which weighs a whopping 180 tons – some 1,600m down a runway.
The Bao 5 is Denza's Land Rover Defender rival, with the boxy 4x4 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) offering 56 miles of EV-only range and 537bhp and 750Nm of torque from its 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine.
As well as pulling the passenger jet using all four wheels, the Chinese family car also became the first production vehicle to tow a plane on two wheels and the first to tow a 747 using electric power alone.
Denza said it set out to achieve something 'hugely ambitious' that 'had never been tried before', and that 'truly challenged the capability of the advanced plug-in hybrid powertrain'.
The Bao 5 went on sale in October and costs from £69,500 – so it doesn't have BYD's bargain price tags on its side. First UK owners are taking delivery now.
To prove the Bao 5's rugged capabilities and the might of its DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) powertrain, the SUV towed the massive aircraft for three runs of Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey.
The first run was on all four wheels, a second on three wheels, and a final run on two wheels – which had never been attempted before.
Over the combined distance of all three runs – which allowed for stops for filming and to remove wheels – the Bao 5 towed the 747 the equivalent of four laps of a standard-size athletics track.
Denza used a standard Bao 5 for the runs: a production-specification car in Ultimate guise with minimal modifications. The DMO plug-in hybrid powertrain was used in its normal form.
A bespoke towing attachment was made to connect the Bao 5 to the aircraft, while the car's passenger seats were removed to facilitate the installation of 4,500kg of ballast when driving with two wheels, and 2,000kg when driving on three wheels.
Additionally, small stabilisers were added to each axle to balance out the removal of the two driven wheels.
The plug-in hybrid SUV pulled the plane using all four wheels, as well as two wheels, and on electric power alone
A standard Bao 5 was used for the runs with minimal modifications. The DMO PHEV powertrain was used in its normal form too
In total the Bao 5 towed the 747 for 1,600 metres - the equivalent of four laps of a standard-size athletics track
Should luxury SUVs be built for extreme feats or focus on practical everyday needs?
The Boeing 747-400 used for the runs left active service in 2020 but still retains its engines and fully furnished interior.
To make matters harder for the Bao 5 – which promises to 'conquer the unexpected' – the weather was typically British with torrential rain arriving for the final attempts.
However, eventually, the runway dried out sufficiently for the car to find enough traction to get the 747 moving.
The incredible feat comes just days after reports emerged that JLR in August had orchestrated a raid on the European offices of Denza's Chinese parent group, BYD, over accusations that its new Ti7 SUV is a dupe of its best-selling Defender SUV.
However, JLR suffered a setback last week when a judge ordered the carmaker to destroy all copies of documents seized , which were deemed not relevant to its copycat claims.
The Denza Bao 5's (left) boxy proportions are very much like those of the popular Land Rover Defender (right). But the Bao 5 as 56 miles of EV range compared to the Defender PHEV's 27 miles
Denza is the BYD brand few people will have heard of.
Founded in China in 2010, the luxury tech arm of BYD focuses on 'new energy vehicles' – EVs and advanced hybrids.
Denza's first model went on sale in China at the end of 2014, and then in 2025 B YD announced that Denza would arrive in Europe, with Britain set to be one of its first markets.
Denza promises to 'blend cutting-edge technology with sophisticated design to deliver a smarter, safer and more refined driving experience'.
Having pinpointed the boxy 4x4 market as its first move in the UK, Denza sees the Bao 5 not only as a Defender adversary, but as an 'entry ticket to the segment'.
The Bao 5 can produce 537bhp and 760nM and can do 0-62mph in 4.8 seconds
Inside the Bao 5 has a 12.3-inch driver display, a 15.6-inch infotainment screen, a wide head-up display and a passenger widescreen as well as cockpit-style buttons
The square-cut SUV has an upright stance, assertive front-end, ring-shaped headlights framing a dark grille, scalloped lower bumper and contrasting skid plate.
But while it's all business on the outside, the cabin is luxurious.
It mixes state-of-the-art tech – a 12.3-inch full-LCD driver display, 50-inch head-up display, 15.6-inch central touchscreen and 12.3-inch passenger display – with soft materials and utilitarian off-roading features.
The cockpit-style button panel and gear selector are paired with practical and durable features in angular grab-handle-style air vents.
As well as the 56 miles of electric-only mode – significantly more than the Defender PHEV's 27-mile EV range – with a full petrol tank and a battery charged to 100 per cent you get 537 miles in total without needing to stop.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump Speaks on China Summit, Trade Deals and Data Centers
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump Speaks on China Summit, Trade Deals and Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday offered unusually warm praise for the top two Democrats in Congress and suggested that the incoming Democratic majority may prove easier to negotiate with than Republicans.
Speaking to reporters in the briefing room, Trump described Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House, as “streetwise” and “smart,” and also praised the current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, a striking change in tone toward two lawmakers with whom he has repeatedly clashed. Trump also said prominent Democrats had already reached out to him privately about making potential deals next year on health care and immigration.
The comments offered one of the clearest indications yet of how Trump intends to navigate a dramatically altered political landscape following the midterm elections, which delivered Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and left the President facing the prospect of two years of legislative gridlock, aggressive congressional investigations, and potentially another effort to impeach him.
Trump appeared eager to present himself as a potential negotiating partner, even as he emphasized that he would use his veto power to block legislation he opposed. He suggested that Democratic leaders might eventually conclude that reaching compromises with him would be more productive than repeatedly passing bills he would reject.
“If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too,” Trump said. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care.”
Trump declined to identify the Democrats who had contacted him, saying only that they were influential figures interested in discussing two of the most contentious domestic policy questions. “I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said. “People that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me about two things in particular: healthcare, because we can do something with healthcare together. Maybe easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation.”
It was not immediately clear whom Trump had spoken with or whether substantive negotiations had begun. Jeffries said earlier this month that he had not spoken with the President since the election.
Still, Trump’s remarks came as Democrats have begun assembling a legislative agenda that will test whether their sweeping electoral victory can translate into tangible policy achievements with a Republican president in the White House.
Health care, in particular, has emerged as a potential area of overlap, though significant disagreements remain over how far the federal government should go in expanding coverage and how to pay for it.
Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take power in January, has proposed a four-year transition toward Medicare for All. His plan would begin by lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expanding benefits to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guaranteeing health coverage for children through age 18.
Jeffries has also indicated a willingness to pursue some of those priorities. This week, he said Democrats were preparing proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand benefits and ensure health coverage for children. He has pledged to move quickly to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republican control.
Sanders has said that Trump might be more receptive than many Republicans assume. "Trump may be crazy, but he's not stupid, and he is a good politician,” Sanders said in a podcast posted to his YouTube page. “If we were to pass something that guaranteed healthcare to all people, that was enormously popular, and Trump says, 'I'm vetoing it.' Not a smart political move.”
Sanders added: "He may say, 'Well, I don't like this or that, let's sit down and negotiate it, but maybe I will sign something.' I think that's a possibility on a lot of legislation, because Trump has no ideology."
Whether Trump would embrace any of those proposals remains uncertain. Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would carry substantial federal costs, and the President has offered no specific commitments to expanding Medicare or reversing Medicaid reductions. But his suggestion that an agreement with Democrats might be easier than advancing legislation through budget reconciliation, a procedure that allows certain measures to bypass the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold, raised the possibility of a bipartisan alternative.
“Can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want,” Trump said. “We could end up with great health care in our country.”
Immigration presents a more complicated opening, particularly given Trump's decision after the election to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, to White House chief of staff. Jeffries denounced Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist,” underscoring the gulf between the Democratic leader and the administration.
Yet Trump has said that his administration's aggressive enforcement policies may have contributed to Republicans' devastating election losses. In a recent interview with 60 Minutes , Trump conceded that deporting immigrants who had lived and worked in the United States for years may have alienated voters who otherwise supported his border security agenda. “I think it might be too tough,” Trump said of his deportation policies. “That hurt me.”
He has suggested that a deal with Democrats could protect certain longtime residents who had committed no crimes beyond entering the country illegally, while preserving his administration's ability to deport people convicted of serious offenses.
This week, Jeffries said the new House majority would move early next year to advance the American Dream and Promise Act, legislation that would provide a path to permanent legal residency for immigrants brought to the United States as children and certain people protected from deportation under Temporary Protected Status.
Trump's friendlier tone toward Jeffries on Friday stood in sharp contrast to his history with the Democrat, whose relationship with the President has been marked by increasingly personal attacks. During a government funding dispute last year, Trump circulated an AI-generated video depicting Jeffries wearing a sombrero, which the Democratic leader denounced as racist and bigoted. Their exchanges grew even more caustic after Trump posted a video depicting former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes, prompting Jeffries to call the president an “unhinged bottom feeder.”
Schumer, by contrast, has a longer personal history with Trump, dating to their years in New York politics. On Friday, Trump recalled giving Schumer what he described as his first political contribution, a $500 donation during an early campaign. “I always had a good relationship until I ran for office,” Trump said. “I was one of his backers.”
“I got richer and richer and richer, and he got more successful politically,” he added. “Who knew this was going to happen?”
Schumer is currently locked in a battle with Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the Majority Leader role, which will be determined on Dec. 1. Jeffries, facing no challenger, was elected the Speaker-designate by House Democrats this week.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock extends $2.7 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock extends $2.7 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.content_orig:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 46% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by about $2.6 trillion. The stock is now trading at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet .
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the  AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday described Russia's actions in Ukraine and Europe as an "irresponsible gamble" that would only increase European resolve. "By escalating its war of aggression against Ukraine and also pursuing an aggressive agenda on European soil, Russia is making an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans, and of all those who want to work towards peace and stability on our continent," he wrote on X.
Macron posted his comments after Moscow hit Ukraine with massive strikes and two Russian missiles appeared to have landed in Poland.
Denmark meanwhile accused Russia of attempting to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on its soil.
US President Donald Trump has defended his admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin while deflecting a reporter's question as to whether the Russian strongman is a friend to the United States or just the president.
"I can't speak to America" but said: "I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with]. It's actually very good."
Trump said the two bonded over the 2016 US presidential election, which Democrats say involved Russian meddling on Trump's behalf , charges that Trump rejects as what he has branded the "Russia hoax."
The US leader also said it will be hard to end the war in Ukraine — something he said he would easily do on his first day back in office nearly two years ago — because of the animosity between Putin and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"It's a very hard thing to do, to be honest. You have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other."
Once again, Trump also claimed, with no real world evidence, that Putin would "love to end the war" that he launched in February 2022, despite the fact that Russia launched massive attacks on neighboring Ukraine as soon as his meeting with Trump and Xi had ended.
US President Donald Trump , fresh back from meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, told reporters on Friday during a one-and-a-half-hour press conference that he had "very good" talks with Putin on Ukraine.
Trump said he could not speak about security guarantees for Kyiv because there was no peace deal in place to end Russia's ongoing invasion after over four and a half years.
But the US president said aggressor Putin — whom Trump proudly called "my friend" when the two met in this week — "clearly expressed his desire to see the war in Ukraine end by diplomatic means."
Trump also did not detail the conditions Moscow would place on Ukraine for such a diplomatic settlement.
On Friday, Russia launched a massive air attack against Ukraine, with two missiles also landing in Poland, a NATO member.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius "welcomed in every respect" a move by Russian President Vladimir Putin to consult Europeans on the future of Ukraine (see entries below for more details).
During a trip to the Polish capital Warsaw, Pistorius added that declining such an invitation to Moscow would send the "completely wrong signal."
"We need to talk. Only by talking can we ultimately achieve results," he said.
Pistorius said reaching an agreement was the goal — not simply sitting down in a room together.
"He [Putin] must now show that he truly means what he says and that he will then take the necessary steps to ensure that, at the very least, a ceasefire is established and that peace-sustaining stability can once again take hold in Europe," the German minister said.
The comments came the same day a pair of Russian missiles and a drone were reported to have violated Polish airspace (see entries below).
While Russian officials said Germany, France and the UK had been invited to send representatives to talks on Ukraine, no details about a time or place for such talks have been announced.
Denmark's PET intelligence service has said it suspected Russia was behind a plot to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper at a Copenhagen concert.
"In our assessment, this case shows that Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out a targeted killing in Denmark," PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told a news conference.
Kieffer-Kristensen added that Russia was suspected of enlisting the help of a local criminal gang for the killing.
The Danish Foreign Ministry subsequently summoned the Russian ambassador and expelled the Russian Embassy's defense attache, Foreign Minister Lars ​Lokke ​Rasmussen said.
The foreign minister also called on European countries to stop issuing visas to Russians and said the Danish government would have taken harsher steps if Russia had a larger diplomatic presence in Denmark.
This week, Ukraine launched a series of strikes on the Kerch bridge , which links occupied Crimea to mainland Russia .
The 19-kilometer (12-mile) bridge has both rail and roadways, part of which has been destroyed in the strikes.
The bridge is widely seen as a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, and damage to it is regarded as a significant psychological blow to Moscow.
Following the strikes, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate and warned the response would be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge, as seen in the sliding image below.
At least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first 10 months of 2026, the United Nations said.
UNICEF , the UN's children's agency, said that between January and October, at least 114 children were killed and 1,030 injured.
The agency said it was the highest number of casualties seen in more than 3 years.
"That is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day" this year, said UNICEF spokeswoman Louise Wateridge.
Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, the UN agency said.
"Attacks involving missiles and armed drones continue to put children and families at risk in their homes, schools, and communities, including far from the frontline," UNICEF warned.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Russia's violation of Polish airspace "utterly unacceptable."
"The incursion into ​Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly," ​Burnham said at an EU-UK ​summit press conference ‌in Brussels.
The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the "Coalition of the Willing" that ​groups allies of Ukraine, including the UK.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the move was a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.
"Europe ​will not be ‌deterred from our support for Ukraine," Streeting said. "We will not allow ⁠Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the ⁠frontline ​in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere."
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has reportedly invited representatives from Germany, France and the UK to Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to Russian news agency Interfax.
"We are waiting for a reply," the diplomat was reported to have said.
On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials would be invited to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
Interfax reported that Ryabkov stressed that such a visit would not automatically mean that European nations would be involved in the negotiations on ending the war on Ukraine.
A statement from the French president's office said Europeans were ready to visit Moscow if given a full role in Ukraine talks.

articles.title_orig: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
articles.title_zh: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
articles.content_orig:
Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion .
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction; Nasdaq erases 2026 gain as AI rout picks up steam
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction; Nasdaq erases 2026 gain as AI rout picks up steam
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.
The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.
Anthropic lost 8.5%, giving back a large chunk of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid more than 13% and around 14%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. It also recorded its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement .
The three leading U.S. indexes experienced a massive sell-off on Friday.
The S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, while the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28% to 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33.
All three major averages were trading below their 200-day moving averages on Friday, and BTIG believes more turmoil could be ahead.
"Generally speaking once something is below a 200 DMA, the risk is to the downside," said Jonathan Krinsky, the firm's chief market technician.
Thursday marked the sixth consecutive day of declines for the S&P 500 , and Krinsky found that over the last 30 years, there are only three prior instances of six-day losing streaks that close below the 200-day moving average but not by more than 3%.
"The 'slightly' good news is that all three saw SPX higher five days later. The not so good news is that all of them saw meaningful downside after that small pop," he said.
When assessing Thursday's performance, Wolfe Research found that the broad market index's "violent" reversal after its attempt to move back to its 200-day moving average at the open was succeeded by the "worst breadth reading" since last December, seeing decliners outnumber advancers by 12:1.
"Broken trends and deteriorating momentum remain significant headwinds," wrote technical analyst Rob Ginsberg in a Thursday note. "The bulls need to mount a powerful defense here to stabilize the market and begin reversing the broader deterioration."
The national average for regular gasoline fell to $3.69 a gallon on Friday, down from $3.72 on Thursday, according to AAA . Prices are still about 59 cents higher than a year ago.
The drop comes ahead of Thanksgiving next week, with 73 million people expected to take road trips.
"It's possible the national average will drop another 15 cents by next Thursday and avoid setting a new record," according to AAA's post.
Brent ​crude futures, the international benchmark, were up 0.64% to $92.57 a barrel on Friday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December rose 0.93% to settle at $83.98 a barrel.
— Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells
Humana shares rose 3% after TD Cowen upgraded the healthcare services company to buy from hold, raising the price target to $485, implying a 28% upside from the stock's Thursday close of $380.
"Taking into account 2026 performance, 2027 Medicare Advantage benefit design and 2028 Stars results, we see a relatively clear path towards a meaningful step-up in 2027 EPS growth and  more than $40 EPS in 2028," the bank said in its note.
Adjusted EPS estimates for 2026, 2027, and 2028 remain unchanged at $9.51, $18.41, and $40.42, respectively.
Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.
Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.
Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.
To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.
Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.
BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's " The Exchange " Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.
He specifically noted Apple , the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he said. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now."
He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.
Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher . The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.
Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.
The day-one moves of Circle , Figma , Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250% .

articles.title_orig: This VIX Signal Is Bullish For The S&P 500
articles.title_zh: This VIX Signal Is Bullish For The S&P 500
articles.content_orig:
There's a bull market... in fear.
Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide tech outages to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering, traders on Tuesday piled into protective put options on the S&P 500 Index at a rate that suggests fear beyond just an AI-specific correction. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged nearly 5 points to a high of 27.7 at the worst of Tuesday's selling and the ratio of put to call volumes on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) hit 1.5, the highest since the first week of April, according to Barchart data. The 'VIX' was last still hovering above 26. With the VIX climbing four days in a row, the volatility gauge hasn't traded under 16 since Oct. 16, arguably trending higher as the S&P 500 slips below this month's lows, trading under 7,300 for the lowest price for the benchmark equity gauge since June. Cboe's three-month volatility gauge, VIX3M, briefly touched the highest since April.
While Nvidia earnings are contributing to the uncertainty – the stock's options currently imply more than a 7% move after its report, the biggest in almost two years – volatility in the S&P 500 jumped more than in the Nasdaq 100 Tuesday, pointing to a more widespread fear among investors. "SPX vol is expanding faster than NDX vol, as SPX vol is coming from a lower base," Eric Metz, CIO, SpiderRock Advisors for BlackRock, said via email. "Today, the market is pricing acute near-term stress in large-caps broadly, but tech-specific fear is still notable. Even within the technology cohort, Tuesday's laggards took on a different tone. Software stocks declined the most ahead of Anthropic's IPO, with options volume on the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) surging to almost four times the 30-day average, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Salesforce was hardest hit, with put contracts outpacing calls on twice the average options volume. "There's a lot of reasons to be risk-off," said Noel Smith, co-CIO of Kai Asset Management. "This is a market-wide phenomenon today that's not just AI stocks." To be sure, bulls weren't totally absent from the session, with the Nasdaq 100 Index holding its November low and VIX still under its Nov. 5 high of 28.4. "While vol is now at a relatively elevated level, we have not seen much fear in the options market," said VolSignals' Matthew Nadel, citing fixed-strike volatility in S&P 500 options, which measures volatility changes across specific options strikes. "We have seen a pretty decent move higher in SPX fixed strike vol, however the move up in vol has been mostly orderly."

articles.title_orig: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.title_zh: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.title_zh: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Urges NYC Customers to Oppose Mamdani-Backed Delivery Bill
articles.title_zh: Amazon Urges NYC Customers to Oppose Mamdani-Backed Delivery Bill
articles.content_orig:
Small-business advocates and workers rallied in Queens on Thursday, urging local politicians to listen to their pleas about the Delivery Protection Act , pending legislation that they said could erase thousands of jobs and small businesses in NYC while incurring costs on customers.
The Queens Chamber of Commerce, delivery workers and small business owners gathered outside the district offices of Queens Council Members, including bill sponsor Tiffany Cabán, to demand meetings about the Delivery Protection Act , which they said could destroy their livelihoods.
“Amazon has already set the precedent in other cities. They’ll just close up shop and move on. They will move out of the city,” Kris Basmagy, owner of Dashwave Delivery, a third-party contractor known as a Delivery Service Provider (DSP) for Amazon, told amNewYork while highlighting Amazon’s Quebec warehouse closure last year.
Basmagy’s company employs nearly 200 people in peak season. He described the legislation, as currently written, as an effort to make it easier for Amazon workers to unionize. While supporters frame the bill as a worker protection measure, Basmagy said most of his employees prefer working under the DSP model.
“We have the data, we have the facts. These are great jobs that people love, and they don’t want to work for Amazon,” he said. “I want a bill that does that. I want a bill that takes on a bad actor who’s not following safety standards and holds them accountable. If we’re doing a good job, we should be rewarded for it. If we’re doing a good job, we should be able to operate.”
Jordan Rodriguez shared how he started working as a DSP delivery driver for Amazon, became a dispatcher and manager, and as of 2024, owns his own DSP company in the Bronx.
“Today, I employ nearly 200 people, many of them whose families are depending on me,” he said. “I’m living the American dream that my parents sacrificed so much for, but today, Intro. 0518 threatens everything I worked to build. I support protecting workers, but please don’t forget the small-business owners and hundreds of families who can be affected by this legislation.”
The Delivery Protection Act, also known as Intro. 0518 would require owners of certain last-mile delivery facilities to be licensed by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and directly employ workers rather than rely on DSPs.
After previous requests to meet have gone unanswered, the group, all part of the New York Delivers Coalition, hand-delivered meeting requests and a letter outlining their concerns on Nov. 19 about the legislation and its potential impact on local jobs and independently owned delivery businesses.
According to the coalition, the legislation would restrict large delivery companies from contracting with DSPs, locally owned businesses that hire and manage delivery workers across New York City. Also, according to the coalition, nearly 80% of the affected workforce lives in the outer boroughs, including 36% in Queens, the largest share of any borough.
Meanwhile, Amazon told its customers on Thursday in a message that the company could add up to $5 per order if the law passes. The company did not say how it arrived at that value.
“The New York City Council is considering Intro. 518, legislation that could increase prices for New Yorkers and affect how Amazon and other companies deliver packages, groceries, and more, to you,” the message stated.
Management further said if the legislation passes, Amazon would no longer be able to work with the DSPs and would be forced to consider moving operations outside of the city.
“That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees,” the company said in a statement. We’re trying to prevent that by working collaboratively with the City Council, and we’ve invited every member to visit our delivery stations and meet with these small businesses and their employees before voting on legislation that could eliminate their businesses, displace thousands of New Yorkers from their jobs, and hurt people who count on fast and affordable delivery every day.”
Caban, the bill’s sponsor, pushed back, calling Amazon’s criticism a “spurious attack. She argued that the proposed legislation would make workers and city streets safer.
“The Delivery Protection Act would require companies like Amazon to pay a $500 licensing fee every other year and comply with basic workplace and public safety regulations,” she said in a statement.
The council member said she does not believe a delivery surcharge would be necessary if the legislation were enacted.
“It’s simply dishonest to claim that this bill would require them to charge consumers $5 for every delivery,” she said. “New Yorkers won’t let themselves be bullied by corporations and billionaires.”
Council Speaker Julie Menin called the surcharge a “deceptive campaign” by Amazon.
“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs,” she said. “If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong.”
Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president of policy, advocacy, and research at economic policy nonprofit Groundwork Collaborative, told amNewYork that Intro. 0518 is important because it would hold Amazon more accountable for its delivery operations, including when workers are injured on the job.
“It is really designed to fix that problem, where, if Amazon controls how and when these people work, it is ultimately responsible for directly employing those workers,” she said. “Right now, Amazon is able to skirt a lot of responsibility for the workers who make its profits possible.”
Among the operations that Amazon controls over DSP workers, including outfits they wear and how fast they work, Pancotti said.
“Amazon gets to control all of that but not take accountability for the consequences,” she said.
As of Nov. 19, Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos was listed as the world’s second-richest billionaire in real time, according to Forbes . His current net worth is $377.3 billion.
Meanwhile, Intro. 0518 has 35 City Council sponsors and remains in the committee on consumer and worker protection.
Barbara Russo-Lennon is a digital editor at amNewYork.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets through Friday, with the S&P 500 down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% by mid-afternoon.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 4% by afternoon trading as shares in major tech companies continued to fall.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing -  with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell off continued.
Nvidia shares had plunged by more than 11% by the afternoon, while Musk's firms SpaceX and Tesla had both fallen by more than 6%.
Meta was down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 3.5%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Trump on Friday offered a defense of ousted Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, but — perhaps more significantly — criticized the new leadership of the chipmaker.
The comments came during a press conference in which the president again praised Huang's role in developing the company's advanced Blackwell chips.
"Jensen did that, and I think there are very few people in that company that can do that," the president said.
"I'm not trying to be disrespectful," Trump added of Huang's replacements. "I watched the people talking about how the company's going to be and where it's going to be." He didn't finish the thought, other than to say of Huang, "I would love to see him be back."
It was a clear reference to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and new board chair Harvey Jones, who took over last week following Huang's resignation and faced some criticism for their presentation on the company's earnings call earlier this week.
Kress took the reins of the company after Huang built close ties with the Trump administration. Huang was often seen in Washington at Trump's side or traveling with the president. He accompanied Trump to China earlier this year.
Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a direct subordinate amid questions about whether he oversaw the evasion of US export controls on advanced semiconductor chips.
Trump has noted Huang's desire to sell chips in China, but said he wants "only older chips" to be available.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said on Friday. "We're a country of second chances."
Trump also showed support for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Friday, saying "I have not lost confidence" in his Cabinet member, whom he called "a different kind of a guy."
"He has a natural business instinct. I think he's done a very good job," Trump said.
Lutnick has been under fire for suggestions that he moved too slowly on the Trump administration's push to crack down on advanced chips from Nvidia and others making their way into Chinese hands.
Tom Cotton of Arkansas, a top Republican senator, told the Wall Street Journal Friday that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings that US chips were being smuggled into China.
Cotton stopped short of saying Lutnick should be fired but declined to support him.
Both Lutnick and Huang are set to testify publicly before lawmakers in the weeks ahead in what could be two of Washington's most closely watched congressional grillings in years.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.
