articles.title_orig: Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
articles.title_zh: Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
articles.content_orig:
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate
H e got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.
The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.
“ Who is he? ” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”
Trump, Xi and Putin convened at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of the US, China and Russia, the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The official product of their 70-minute closed-door meeting was a four-point document titled the “Declaration Toward Peace” that made no mention of the wars in Iran or Ukraine.
But the defining image was of the trio sitting around a huge circular wooden table. At its hollow centre sat an immaculate arrangement of pink flowers, an ancient Chinese motif meant to evoke harmony. To US-based critics, however, the optics sent a different signal.
Steve Schmidt , a former adviser to George W Bush and John McCain, said: “The image of the grotesque large round table with a war criminal dictator, a stable dictator and an irrational, delusional wannabe dictator is an image of deep shame and weakness for the United States.
“It’s a repudiation of American values, American honour, common sense and the national security interests of the country, and a betrayal of America’s allies all across the world.”
Beijing understood how to satisfy the Trump ego. When Air Force One landed in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, Xi made the unusual move of greeting Trump personally on the tarmac. An honour guard stood at attention, crowds waved miniature US and Chinese flags, schoolchildren shook pompoms and Xi drew Trump into a warm embrace.
Trump took the bait with delight. For him, victory was not measured in negotiating concessions but in the lavish banquet and the seat reserved for him at the head table. “That’s a big win for us,” he said in a TV interview. “It’s a big win for China too. We get along.” Trump was even treated to a performance of YMCA, the signature song of his campaign rallies.
In their first meeting since failed negotiations in Alaska last year, Trump held one-on-one talks with Putin that touched on Ukraine but secured no immediate commitments. The meeting occurred against a backdrop of Trump recently rejecting new sanctions on Russia.
In a bilateral meeting with Xi, Trump raised the US-led war in Iran, emphasising a joint interest in fully reopening the strait of Hormuz and preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Xi focused on US-China trade stability and asserted China’s sovereign position on Taiwan, treating it as an unalterable domestic issue.
In one ominous remark, Trump told Xi: “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem.” He later told NBC News that the pair had also agreed that artificial intelligence needed some form of safety “guardrails” but offered few details.
The main event was the trilateral summit, with observers watching body language closely for any clues about the dynamics among Xi, relishing his role as host, Putin, whose war in Ukraine is faltering, and Trump, ostensibly the most powerful of the three but politically wounded at home. To many, it offered little more than a glorified photo op.
Brett Bruen , the president of the public affairs agency Global Situation Room and the former global engagement director of the Barack Obama White House, said: “Brand Trump has been badly sullied by a historic defeat at the hands of American voters. However, this isn’t going to improve his standing internationally and certainly not domestically.
“If anything, it put on display his desperation. It put on display his isolation internationally from the very people that he’s going to need to be able to secure trade deals or peace deals. Once again he’s returning from China with the luggage hold empty of any diplomatic accomplishments.”
The formal output of the summit was a study in profound omissions and authoritarian wishlists. The text made no mention of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, nor of the spiralling US military conflict with Iran.
Instead, the trio agreed on four broad points: pledging dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, committing to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum, calling for “reforms” to the United Nations and declaring that state sovereignty and the immunity of state officials must be respected while warning that the international criminal court (ICC) must not abuse its jurisdiction.
Putin currently faces an active ICC arrest warrant for war crimes in Ukraine, while the Trump administration has sanctioned ICC officials to shield itself and its ally Israel from judicial scrutiny.
Ned Price , a former deputy to the US representative to the UN, said: “The joint statement was notable, not because Russia and China said it, but because the United States also co-signed.
“The United Nations they want is not a United Nations that’s more effective but rather a United Nations that is less effective at upholding the rules of the road, the very principles that have been at the centre of the UN system since its founding: the idea that big countries can’t bully small countries, that borders can’t be redrawn by force.”
The talks have done little to dispel the impression that Trump regards Congress, the media and elections as pesky encumbrances while gazing with awe and some envy at Xi and Putin. As the Shenzhen summit concluded, European leaders and Nato officials convened urgently in Berlin to reinforce their support for Ukraine and resist any high-level partitioning of European security.
The summit was a propaganda win for Putin, who went from international pariah status to equal billing with the world’s two biggest economies. It was also a victory for Xi. Without making any concessions on Taiwan, trade tariffs or its industrial lifeline to Moscow, China positioned itself as the arbiter of 21st-century diplomacy.
“Xi was able to burnish China’s diplomatic sway and give Putin and Trump something that each leader respectively coveted,” said Ali Wyne , senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group. “He gave Putin the opportunity to demonstrate that despite Russia’s wartime losses, despite western sanctions, Russia remains a great power.
“He gave Trump the opportunity to demonstrate, at least in Trump’s own mind, that despite these bruising midterm elections, Trump is a singularly visionary and consequential peacemaker, thereby appealing to Trump’s ego.”
While neither Beijing nor Moscow harbours any illusions about Trump’s volatile temperament, both recognise the ticking clock on his second term and know they are likely to outlast him.
Wyne added: “Both of them recognise that it is next to impossible that any of President Trump’s successors will view them in comparable terms as friends, adopt conciliatory dispositions, and on certain issues come close to aligning US positions with those of China and Russia.”
Although he was caught on camera apparently nodding off, Trump departed China appearing politically rejuvenated after his encounters with his two “friends”. He hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media and said later: “On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12.”

articles.title_orig: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.title_zh: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says next move on Iran may not come until 2027 as Tehran denies chemical weapons claim
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile Friday, causing a fire onboard the vessel but no injuries, according to a British naval monitor.
The tanker was traveling out of the key waterway when it was struck by an unknown projectile, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.
The UKMTO earlier reported that a bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, had reported shots being fired in its vicinity by assailants on a small boat.
During Friday's news conference, President Trump said that during his trilateral with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping, the three leaders discussed nuclear responsibilities.
Mr. Trump said they "spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet" and that "in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
As he lauded slightly lower gas prices during a news conference at the White House on Friday, President Trump said the U.S. wants a "real deal" with Iran, not a "fake" deal.
"They want to make a deal but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," he said.
"They've been bulls******g people for 51 years," the president said of Iran.
U.S. Central Command denied carrying out any new strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island on Friday after Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is closely linked with the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said a missile had hit the island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tasnim said it had no information of any possible damage, and other Iranian media outlets offered more vague details. The semi-official Fars news agency said an explosion was heard in the skies over the island, but that the cause was unknown.
The U.S. has attacked the island several times, most recently on Tuesday with what a military official described to CBS News as precision strikes on an IRGC missile site.
The official said that strike was launched "in self-defense … in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Friday that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's government in the impoverished nation's more than decade-long civil war against the Iran-backed rebel group.
The latest missiles launched by the Houthis targeted the Jazan region, on the southwest Saudi coast near the border with Yemen, but "air defense intercepted and destroyed" them, according to coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki.
The Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district earlier this week.
A bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, has reported shots being fired in its vicinity by armed men on a small boat, according to a British naval monitor.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, which is run by the British navy, said Friday that the ship was traveling eastbound when it was approached "by a dark blue skiff with six unidentified, armed persons on board."
"Four shots were fired in quick succession from the skiff and warning shots were returned by the armed security team onboard the bulk carrier," UKTMO said, adding that there was no damage reported to the vessel or its crew.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district Friday as the group issued a series of threats against Saudi Arabia.
"We announce that (King Abdullah Financial District) in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, is a military target for our forces. We therefore call on all employees, workers and citizens to stay away from it immediately," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
In a Telegram post Friday, Saree wrote: "We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries. Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of damaging a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district with a strike earlier this week.
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions .
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.
The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.
For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in the escalating conflict with Iran's Houthi allies warned civilians Friday to leave the area around the key port of Hodeidah on Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has been held by the rebels for years.
The warning, issued in a social media post by the coalition's Saudi spokesman, suggested Saudi airstrikes on the port could be imminent. It came after Houthi authorities accused Saudi forces of killing 19 people earlier Friday with an attack that hit a civilian boat.
Yemen's civil war flared back up in July as the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran sent regional tension soaring. While the Yemen war started more than a decade ago with the Iran-backed Houthis seizing a huge portion of the country, including capital city Sanaa, it had been relatively calm for years until this summer.
Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi on Friday accused Saudi forces of a "horrific massacre" for the strike on the boat, which the rebels say killed civilians who had been displaced from their homes by the war.

articles.title_orig: Wall St ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
articles.title_zh: Wall St ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Nasdaq and the Dow erased their 2026 gains and the S&P 500 tumbled to cap brutal week for U.S. stocks
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and the Dow, while the broad S&P 500 entered correction territory, meaning it has declined 10% from its October peak.
The declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip as the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth. Also pushing markets lower was Nvidia, whose stock fell about 14% after a Reuters report indicated that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The losses sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and a frozen jobs market, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. Thanks to the AI investment wave, investors showed a seemingly insatiable demand for stocks, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
But while Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weeks-long slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices , rising interest rates , mounting corporate debt loads , stubborn inflation , supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories that raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout, and received a fresh jolt last week as the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sent shares in a company at the heart of that buildout tumbling.
Alongside the stock sell-off, there has been an increase in purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn.
Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said.
“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify publicly when he appears before the Senate banking panel, a spokesperson for Committee Chair Tim Scott said Friday.
The South Carolina Republican confirmed earlier this week that Huang had agreed to appear, but the details of that appearance remained unclear. Huang, who resigned from the company he co-founded earlier this month over a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, also reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
The date of Huang's public testimony in the Senate has not yet been announced, though Scott initially requested he appear on Dec. 3.
His office did not respond when asked when Huang would appear. Scott told CNBC on Wednesday he hopes to hear testimony from Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "before Christmas." The new Congress, when Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., is expected to take over as Senate banking chair, convenes Jan. 3.

UnitedHealth Group has sued the federal government over its lowered Medicare Advantage star ratings for next year, further plunging the program’s ratings system into disarray.
UnitedHealth marks at least the 15th Medicare Advantage plan to file a lawsuit against the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for how the agency calculated 2027 star ratings. UnitedHealth is also the largest Medicare Advantage insurer, covering more than 9 million people. Medicare’s annual enrollment period ends Dec. 7.
The government rates Medicare Advantage plans on a scale from one to five stars, based on health screens, customer satisfaction, and other measures that get mixed into a complicated formula. Those with at least four stars earn bonus money. The insurers argue in their lawsuits that the government’s measurement is inconsistent and is inappropriately dropping their scores below the bonus thresholds.

articles.title_orig: Raft of departures could hit WCCO as CBS buyout deadline arrives
articles.title_zh: Raft of departures could hit WCCO as CBS buyout deadline arrives
articles.content_orig:
Multiple employees at WBZ-TV (Channel 4) have decided to take voluntary buyouts as part of a cost-cutting move across its parent company Skydance.
Chief investigative reporter Cheryl Fiandaca, reporter Kristina Rex, and meteorologist Jacob Wycoff are among the staff that have informed the station that they have accepted a buyout, according to people who are familiar with the decisions but were not authorized to discuss them publicly.
“As previously reported, voluntary buyout offers were made available to eligible employees across the company,” a CBS Stations spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognize the interest in learning which anchors and reporters may be leaving our local stations. These are deeply personal decisions, and we want to approach each departure with the respect, care and gratitude our colleagues deserve.”
The deadline to accept the offer was Nov. 18, and the company anticipates that the last working day for staffers taking the buyout will be Dec. 4.
“SAG-AFTRA is advocating on behalf of our members throughout this process and declines to comment,” said Pamela Greenwalt, chief communications and marketing officer of SAG-AFTRA, which represents on-air anchors and reporters at WBZ-TV.
Employees at the station got buyout offers in the last several weeks as part of a program across Skydance , which is pushing to cut $6 billion over the next three years. Skydance, which is run by David Ellison, acquired Warner Bros. Discovery last month. The massive merger came a year after the media company closed its deal to buy Paramount, which gave it control of CBS News and its local stations, including WBZ-TV.
The buyouts are a “one-time offer,” according to the message sent to employees who met the criteria for the buyouts and requested additional details. The message was obtained by the Globe.
“If you choose to move forward, a formal separation agreement will be sent to you on or before your last day of work outlining your separation benefits, based on your confirmed end date,” the message read. “We value the contributions you have made during your time here, and we want you to feel supported and informed as you consider your decision.”
This round of buyouts differed in that it included an offer to buy on-air staff out of their contracts, on top of offering severance based on years of service, according to an offer reviewed by the Globe. The offer means that some long-time staff in multi-year contracts were eligible for years of separation compensation.
The agreement also waived all conditions of employee contracts with the exception of employees who had a noncompete provision, which WBZ said it would waive “only after a period of 30 days after the separation date.”
The cuts are just the latest at WBZ, which bought out photographers and laid off staff last year. Among the departures were Dr. Mallika Marshall, who said she was laid off, and Beth Germano, who retired. Political analyst Jon Keller was also laid off, but rejoined the station as a special contributor in March.

articles.content_orig:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK
The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.
Burnham ‌said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029 , but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year ‌with the EU about what could be achieved next.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, ‌the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.
However, one potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students. Britain ⁠prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.
Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported. The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.
Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, said the deal “was about the first steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I am ready for this fight,” he said.
Meanwhile, Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending. Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you”, he said.
He also added Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
The UK prime minister called the newly agreed post-Brexit reset deal a “win-win” for the UK and the EU, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
The prime minister met Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at the EU-UK summit in Brussels.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed that Andy Burnham’s reset agreements with the EU “was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024”.
He also said Burnham’s actions “went completely against the pledge that he made to the voters of Makerfield just a few months ago”.
The Reform leader later added: “Burnham’s whole rationale is 73% of the people want to be closer to Europe .
“Well, if you ask me do I want better relations with our European neighbours? Do I think we could have a better trade deal than we’ve got at the moment? I am part of that 73%.
“But what he completely misunderstands is that is not an open ticket to rejoin a significant chunk of the single market today.”
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.
Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.
It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.
An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.
A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.
Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.
After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests , governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.

He said: “There is a clear democratic mandate for what has been done today. It’s in the Labour manifesto… There will be nothing beyond the significance of this in this parliament.”

Mr. Trump called Stephen Miller, his new chief of staff and longtime aide, up to the lectern. Miller claimed the president over the last two years has achieved "more than any president has achieved by far in American history."
"No president has done what he has done over the last two years," Miller said. "What you're going to see over the next two years — as astonishing as that has been — under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history."
After Miller left the podium, Mr. Trump asked, "Do you want to run for president?"
He later praised Miller as "a talent" and said he has "a big heart."
"A lot of people think he doesn't," Mr. Trump said.
The president said he has not lost confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, despite a rift between Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and others in the administration about how to handle chips going to China. Republicans on Capitol Hill have been calling for Lutnick to testify and answer their questions.
"I have not lost confidence," the president said, calling Lutnick a "different" kind of guy, perhaps not like Bessent, whom the president said is out of "central casting." The president called Lutnick a "natural" businessman.
"It's different folks, right?" Mr. Trump said.
The president said he received a phone call from Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, claiming she wants to have a "strong border."
"I received a phone call from the new governor, governor-elect of Texas," Mr. Trump said. "She was really nice. It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border. And I think we'll be able to work something out."
Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by about seven points.
Asked about reports that Iran is developing plans to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C., the president said he's heard that "rumor" but his administration won't let it happen.
"There is a rumor that they're building a dirty bomb," the president said, insisting the U.S. knows what the Iranians are doing.
"We know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," he said.
Mr. Trump said he plans to veto Democratic-led legislation over the next two years unless Democrats work with him on his priorities.
"They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them. And then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them," he said.
Mr. Trump said he would eventually give Democrats an ultimatum: "I'm going to say, I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this."
"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too," he said, adding that he's open to working with Democrats on healthcare and other legislation.
The president would not say whether he has spoken yet with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become House speaker early next year. But he called the New York Democrat "a smart guy."
"He's a streetwise guy," he said.
Mr. Trump said corporate system outages across the country are all separate issues, company by company.
"They're all separate events," he said.
The president said thousands of companies are upgrading their systems right now. "And when they upgrade, bad things happen," he said.
"I have a very good understanding of what we're talking about," the president said of AI and company systems. The president insisted the companies will fix it all soon.
The director of national intelligence suggested this week that the outages resulted from software patches and upgrades. The FAA groundstop, however, likely resulted from a hardware issue.
The president called the air traffic control system "ancient."
Mr. Trump said he wants Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang leading the company again, calling him "one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world."
"I would love to see him back," he said, adding that Huang should "be given a second chance."
"I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back because he created something with Blackwell," he said, referring to the company's most advanced AI chip.
"You can't copy the chip because it's so advanced and so complex that it can't be copied. And Jensen did that, and I think there are very few people in that company that can do that."
Mr. Trump said Huang's work has put the U.S. 10 years ahead of other countries when it comes to AI chips.
"I think the company, if they were smart, they [would] take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work," Mr. Trump said.
The president said having a good relationship with Putin and Russia gives the U.S. additional strength, appearing to express sympathy for Putin over the war that the Russian president began and continues to wage in Ukraine.
Mr. Trump said Putin was "very nice" about what he described as the fake Russia "hoax," referring to allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign colluded with Moscow.
"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship," the president said. "And it's actually very good. He's got lots of nuclear — he's second to us in nuclear weapons, it's very good. I think it, I think it gives us a lot of additional strength. And he's having a hard time right now because he's in a war that should have lasted one day and it's lasted for five years."
After Putin left the meetings in China, Russia launched more attacks on Ukraine, despite Mr. Trump saying Russia wants to end the war.
"You're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.
Mr. Trump denied that he was upset with Vance over a statement he put out after the election that blamed GOP losses on the conflict.
As the question was being asked, Rubio caught Vance's eye and shook his head.
"I didn't say I was unhappy with it. I thought the statement was fine," Mr. Trump said. "It was a very accurate statement."
But he said he would "absolutely" do it again, adding that the war drove up fuel prices "far less than I thought."
In a post on X the day after Election Day, Vance said many Trump voters backed Democrats this election because of the Iran war, cost of living and inflation and the U.S. relationship with Israel.
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Speaking after the president, Vance also praised the bipartisan bill to overhaul permitting as "amazing," saying it will "allow the United States to build like we've never built before."
"That means more homes, more factories, more power plants," Vance said, connecting the Senate-passed legislation to Mr. Trump's trip abroad. "But that doesn't matter unless you create more incentives in the global economy for people to invest in the United States of America."
"So what we saw last week was two really big wins for the American people: the trade deals, but also the major piece of legislation," Vance said. "It's going to pay dividends for the American people."
Mr. Trump said the relationship between him, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin is "fantastic."
The president said he was unaware it was the first trilateral meeting of the U.S., China and Russian heads of state until the press reported it.
"First ever trilateral," he said. "I never knew that. You reported it. And I said, 'if they report it, it must make sense.'"
"It was great, great electricity," he added. "Unbelievable. And the relationship is fantastic between the three of us."
They discussed the "responsibility" that comes with being the world's three largest nuclear powers, he said.

Friday, November 20 @ 1:40 PM ET: A Microsoft spokesperson shared an official statement discussing the upcoming changes. That statement has been added to this piece in its own section.
Users of one of Microsoft’s best free apps will have to add “find a new to do list app” to their list of tasks. But they shouldn’t do so on Microsoft To Do, since all versions of the app are now destined for retirement.
Microsoft To Do will be retired on June 30, 2027 . While the apps will shut down on that date, the underlying To Do service, APIs, and related synchronization support will retire later on separate timelines. Microsoft detailed its plans in a support document . The writing was on the wall that Microsoft To Do was not a priority at Microsoft. The software felt like abandonware, rarely receiving updates or new features. Not that a task tracking app should require many updates, but the Microsoft To Do webpage still uses an icon from Windows 10.
Just a few months ago our Ben Wilson pleaded with Microsoft to keep Microsoft To Do around . His worry that the app would be moved to the Microsoft Graveyard became a reality quickly. Microsoft has focused on Planner recently, and that will be the path forward for business and education users who want to sync tasks across devices and platforms. Planner is not available for personal users.
Even those who switch to Planner will have extra work to do, since tasks will not migrate from Microsoft To Do to Planner.
Microsoft To Do was made by the Wunderlist team after Microsoft acquired that popular application. Wunderlist had a passionate user base and Microsoft To Do earned praise for its swift performance and cross-device syncing. Microsoft eventually shut down Wunderlist and pushed users to Microsoft To Do when the latter was ready for mainstream use.
Microsoft To Do has served as a natural extension to the Microsoft 365 ecosystem for years. Its integration with Outlook felt like magic when it was new. With Microsoft To Do set for retirement, users will have to look for alternatives. I’d recommend Todoist or TickTick as replacements for Microsoft To Do. Google Keep and Apple Reminders are also strong candidates depending on the platforms you use. It’s frustrating to see Microsoft To Do placed on a path to retirement. It’s a useful app that performs well on the web, Windows 11, iOS, and Android. I’d argue it was the pinnacle of Microsoft’s cross-platform app strategy.
After publication, Microsoft shared the following statement regarding Microsoft To Do's retirement. The company reiterated that Planner is the future for work and school users, while personal users will be able to export their data.
“We're bringing task management experiences together across Microsoft 365 to make it easier for customers to manage individual tasks and team plans. As part of this transition, Microsoft To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027 , with work and school experiences coming together in Microsoft Planner . Existing integrations across Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, will also be updated to work with Planner. We recognize this change will affect customers differently, particularly those using personal Microsoft accounts , and we're committed to helping them prepare. Customers will be able to export their To Do data before retirement , and we'll share additional guidance to support the transition." – Howard Crow, Director of Product, Agents and AI , Microsoft (emphasis added).
In short, personal users are not being given a replacement. They are being given an export button.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.content_orig:
Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War
When drones and missiles collapsed a bridge connecting Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, Ukraine's military declared: "The symbol of the occupation has cracked."
Hours later, at a summit held a continent away, an angry-looking Vladimir Putin immediately vowed to end any prospect of peace with Ukraine.
"There will be no agreements. We will respond," he said on the sidelines of the APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen .
But one expert says the bridge's destruction is a "huge blow to Putin's credibility as Russian leader" in a war his country appears to be losing.
The Crimean Bridge, which was constructed in 2016 after Russian forces occupied the Ukrainian peninsula in defiance of international law. ( Reuters: Alexey Pavlishak )
Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula extends south from the country's mainland into the Black Sea.
It has been occupied by Russian forces in defiance of international law since 2014.
Access is via two main roads to the north and the Crimean Bridge, from Crimea's east coast to the Russian mainland further east.
The northern roads lead into Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory that frequently comes under attack from the Ukrainian military.
The 19-kilometre Crimean Bridge, with separate road and rail links running over the Kerch Strait to connect the peninsula to Russia's Krasnodar region, provides the only other road and rail traffic.
It is also a vital road and rail artery connecting the Black Sea with the Azov Sea to the bridge's north.
Russia has relied on the bridge to maintain access to Crimea throughout the current war.
Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition
On Tuesday, local time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced his military had performed what he described as a wartime masterstroke strike weeks in the making.
He said Ukrainian forces knocked out defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching a final attack using long-range drones on the bridge's road section.
At the same time, Neptune missiles targeted the railway, before precision-guided Flamingo missiles were also fired at the bridge.
The bridge is Europe's longest and a source of pride among some Russians. ( Reuters: Supplied/Vantor )
Videos later shared by Mr Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military appeared to show key moments from the attack, with one of the bridge's arches fallen while part of its deck was in the water.
Crimea's Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed the attack halted traffic but said the rail track had been restored. He did not reveal the extent of damage to the bridge.
Malcolm Davis, a senior defence analyst with the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the bridge's collapse reinforces a message Ukraine has declared since 2014: "Crimea does not belong to Russia."
"By cutting off access … It signifies to the world that Putin does not control Crimea, that Crimea is part of Ukraine, and reinforces the fact that Russia is certainly not winning this war," he told the ABC.
"It is certainly a major setback to Putin … That's a huge blow to Putin's credibility as Russian leader."
The Crimean Bridge is Europe's longest, and a source of considerable pride for Russia.
Construction began in 2016, despite strong objections from Ukraine, and was completed in little over two years.
Putin drove across it at its formal opening on May 15, 2018, but for Ukrainians, the bridge remains the most visible and persistent reminder of the Kremlin's claim over the Crimean Peninsula.
Vladimir Putin formally opened the bridge in 2018. ( Reuters: Alexander Nemenov/Pool )
This week's strikes were also not the first launched by Ukraine in opposition to the Russian occupation.
In October 2022, Moscow said a truck bomb had been used to target the bridge, temporarily halting road and rail traffic.
Two months later, Putin walked over the repaired road.
Vladimir Putin walked on the bridge's newly repaired roadway after it came under attack by Ukrainian forces in 2022. ( Reuters: Supplied/Sputnik/Mikhail Metzel )
The following year, it came under fire again in attacks by two maritime drones that killed two people, according to Russia's Investigative Committee.
Dr Davis said the latest strikes could be the most significant yet.
"What happens is that the Russian forces on Crimea ultimately start losing effectiveness in the coming weeks," he said.
"[It] makes it easier for the Ukrainians, if they wanted to, to try and recapture Crimea in the future."
In China, Mr Putin claimed the Crimean Bridge had been used exclusively for civilian purposes, rather than to ship military equipment and petrol to Russia's frontline troops.
In the wake of the attack, Russian-installed authorities in Crimea said a ferry service to the Russian mainland would start on Friday, local time, to maintain deliveries of food, medicine and fuel for the peninsula's nearly 2.5 million inhabitants.
Marat Khusnullin, a Russian government vice-premier, told state TV he believed it would take about a week to establish how long repairs would take.
But Inger Kroon, a structural engineering specialist, told Reuters the task of replacing the roughly 227-metre road span and its arch could take more than a year.
The attack came as both Russia and Ukraine were awaiting confirmation of a date for another round of US-mediated peace talks, aimed at ending the war between the two nations.
And while US President Donald Trump said he planned to discuss the war during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Mr Putin in China, no concrete decision on peace came from the talks.
Dr Davis said he did not believe Russia was ever seriously committed to peace negotiations, and expected Mr Putin to "retaliate with massive attacks" against Ukraine.
"This is a bad defeat for the Russians," he said.
"But the war will continue. There's no sign of this coming to an end any time soon."

articles.title_orig: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math
An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology’s year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion
By Joseph Howlett edited by Claire Cameron
vectorfusionart via Shutterstock
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM.
“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website.
The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. It’s one of the few open problems on which the Clay Mathematics Institute has placed a million-dollar bounty. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes.
Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct.
If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. The announcement comes just a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market.
Alpöge says his proof confirms the “Generalized Riemann Hypothesis,” a gargantuan expansion on Riemann’s initial guess that undergirds the entire mathematical universe with untold hidden structure. There is no superlative strong enough for how this would transform mathematics, instantly unlocking a deluge of truths contingent upon the ambitious conjecture.
“If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial,” says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. “Something like a Rosetta Stone.”
The work could open whole new areas of research. "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," says mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
Alpöge’s statement is elegiac—recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling—but also optimistic. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light,” he wrote, “but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”
The Anthropic mathematician has been the subject of headlines since he tweeted a Claude-generated solution to the famous Jacobian conjecture in July, kicking off math’s unprecedented summer. He was central to September’s Navier-Stokes controversy involving OpenAI, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had stolen his and Alpöge’s work.
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn’t have any immediate real-world applications—it won’t upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: “An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I’d want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems.”
“This is indeed an historic moment,” Sutherland told me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean. “The world has changed… I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.” It’s worth celebrating, Sutherland says, the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs—and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today’s advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred “is going to take some time.” “There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he says. “And I can’t wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”
This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Our editors and reporters are often experts in their fields, which means they understand the nuances of big discoveries and can untangle the breakthroughs from the hype. With a subscription, you are also supporting rigorous fact-checking to ensure the words we publish are precise and accurate. And you’re supporting original illustrations, graphics and photos that bring you closer to an advanced laboratory, an ice sheet in Antarctica or a space mission in orbit. You’re helping us craft other types of high-quality journalism as well: Our newsletters are carefully written, edited and curated by staffers you have or will come to know and love. Our Science Quickly podcast is based on original reporting, collaboration with editors and scientists and exacting production.

articles.title_orig: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.title_zh: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.content_orig:
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.
The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.
The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.
Gemini for Home was announced last year , so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year ). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

articles.title_orig: A visual tour of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’s’ stunningly realized Miami
articles.title_zh: A visual tour of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’s’ stunningly realized Miami
articles.content_orig:
CEDAR KEY, Fla. (WCJB) - The developers of “Grand Theft Auto VI” used the iconic seaside City of Cedar Key in North Central Florida as inspiration for one of the game’s locations.
GTA 6 brings players back to the fictional U.S. state of Leonida and Vice City, Rockstar Games’ fictional version of Miami and South Florida. Game designers used real-world locations in Florida as inspiration.
Dock Street and other iconic parts of Cedar Key are recreated in the game’s Watson Bay. Resident Michael Presley Bobbitt recorded a walk-through of the location, pointing out real-world locations.
“This is such a cool, unique place. Who would have ever thought that a fishing village of 700 people would be on the global stage? Come and check it out, friends,” Bobbitt said.
Leaders with the Cedar Key Chamber of Commerce said they hope the game could drive tourism to the island.
“If you live here, you’re connected with every one of those buildings, so it was fun to pick out what’s changed since it was shot, but I will say getting Cedar Key on the map that way is a whole new audience for us, so we kind of love it,” said Tara Barney, a chamber of commerce board member.
A landmark resembling the Ocala Drive-In Theater also appears in the game. A flea market is connected to the business in the game, just like its counterpart in real life.
The Ocala Drive-In Theater is one of only four left in the state.
The owner addressed rumors last month, as previously reported, that his family business was closing down. He said they may sell at some point in the future, but the business is still open.

Following the Android deprecation in September, Google Assistant is going away on speakers and smart displays next year. Additionally, Google Home is fully replacing the Nest app in January.

Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:
With home.nest.com going away, you have to download any custom video clips since they will not transfer over to Google Home. A one-click “Download All” button is available.
Terrible news. For all my first-gen Nest cameras (wired hello doorbell, wired outdoor cams, and multiple indoor cams), I vastly prefer the Nest app to the terrible Google Home app.
Otherwise, Nest app users do not need to do anything else, with devices automatically transferring over to the Google Home app. No Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke alarms, or locks are losing support with this change.
Additionally, Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions will automatically switch to Google Home Premium “with no additional cost and no credit card re-entry required at this time.”
The other change announced today is that Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays is going away on August 2, 2027. It will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant. Google notes that natural language support replaces “rigid, static and highly specific voice commands.” Additionally:
You can upgrade to Gemini today , while Google is expanding international availability over the coming months. Google will share more updates closer to the deadline.

articles.title_zh: S&P 500 Is Set for Longest Losing Run Since 2020: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 4.3% and was down 1.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 traded down 2.9%, while the blue-chip Dow fell 573 points, or 1.2%. Both the S&P 500 and Dow were more than 10% below their closing records.
Anthropic lost 10%, giving back most of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid 12% and more than 11%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. Micron Technology dropped more than 13%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained 2%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose more than 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow has fallen 7%, putting it on pace for its worst weekly performance since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement . The S&P 500 has decreased almost 8%, while the Nasdaq is down about 9%, with both also headed for their largest one-week pullbacks in more than a year.
Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.
Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.
Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.
To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.
Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.
BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's " The Exchange " Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.
He specifically noted Apple , the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he said. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now."
He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.
Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher . The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.
Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.
The day-one moves of Circle , Figma , Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250% .
Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here."
He added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.
— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio
The VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.
The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.
"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in remarks delivered in Chile.
"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households."
Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
The tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.
Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.
The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.
Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.
The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.
